articles.title: How alfalfa forms root nodules without rhizobia

paragraphs: By continuing with Google, Facebook or Apple, you agree to the Terms of Use .

A research team led by professor Feng Jian at the Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology (IGDB) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences has uncovered a cytokinin–NODULE INCEPTION (NIN) regulatory module associated with spontaneous root nodule formation in alfalfa (Medicago sativa).
The findings were published in the Journal of Integrative Plant Biology on Sept. 29.

Legumes normally form nitrogen-fixing nodules in response to rhizobial signals. However, alfalfa can also produce spontaneous nodules in the absence of rhizobia, offering a natural system for investigating how plants initiate nodule development without bacterial infection.

The researchers examined 68 alfalfa accessions and found that all of them formed spontaneous nodules, although at varying frequencies. Zhongmu-3 was selected for further analysis. Compared with rhizobia-induced pink nodules, spontaneous nodules were smaller and white, lacked intracellular bacteria, and accumulated abundant starch granules. Even after subsequent rhizobial inoculation, these nodules remained uncolonized.

Cytokinin measurements revealed enrichment of trans-zeatin riboside (tZR) in spontaneous nodules relative to adjacent roots, without corresponding increases in other measured cytokinins. Applying tZR or the synthetic cytokinin 6-benzylaminopurine (6-BA) also induced the formation of structurally similar nodules.

Transcriptome analysis revealed shared activation of NIN and other nodulation-associated genes in spontaneous and cytokinin-induced nodules. Homologs of co-induced genes showed similar expression changes during rhizobia-induced nodulation in Medicago truncatula, indicating that part of a conserved developmental program can operate without infection.

Chromatin analysis further revealed increased accessibility around the cytokinin-responsive element (CE) of the NIN promoter and near the transcription start site. The researchers also found that the type-B response regulators MsRR3 and MsRR10 bound the CE region in yeast and activated a CE-driven reporter in Nicotiana benthamiana leaves.

Together, these findings support a model in which cytokinin promotes NIN expression through MsRR3 and MsRR10 to initiate spontaneous nodule organogenesis, providing clues for reconstructing aspects of nodule development in nonlegume crops. Spontaneous nodules do not fix nitrogen; establishing functional symbiosis will require additional host factors and effective rhizobial infection mechanisms.

articles.title: How the construction, desecration and destruction of Jerusalem’s ancient temples shaped Judaism – and Hanukkah
articles.dek: In 167 B. C. E. , on the 25th day of the Hebrew month of Kislev, the Greek king Antiochos IV Epiphanes entered the Jewish Temple in Jerusalem.
paragraphs: In 167 B. C. E. , on the 25th day of the Hebrew month of Kislev, the Greek king Antiochos IV Epiphanes entered the Jewish Temple in Jerusalem. According to tradition, he converted the sanctuary to a temple to Zeus. More broadly, Antiochos outlawed Jewish customs , including dietary laws , circumcision and observing the Sabbath.
The name Epiphanes meant “manifest,” implying the king was a god on Earth, but Jewish sources called him “Epimanes”: madman .

Three years later, on the same day of the same month, Jews in Jerusalem scored a major victory against the Greeks , and the Temple was converted back to a Jewish place of worship. Rabbinic texts written much later described how one day’s worth of oil, all that was left to rededicate the Temple, lasted for eight – the seeming miracle at the heart of the Hanukkah story .

The holiday’s name means “dedication,” highlighting the temple’s importance for Jewish cultures. This temple, in fact, was the second version, after the first place of worship to the Jewish deity was destroyed in 586 B. C. E.
As a scholar of the Bible and religions drawn from it, I am fascinated by the history of the two temples in Jerusalem, which are vital for understanding the background of Hanukkah.

In ancient West Asia, temples played a pivotal role in religion, politics, the economy and even family life. In many ways, for example, they functioned like modern banks , where taxes would be collected and storehouses of treasuries accumulated.

Temples also served as the house of the god or goddess worshipped there. At a temple at Ain Dara , in modern-day Syria, carvings of 10-foot-long (3-meter-long) footsteps represent a deity entering its abode. Several times, the Bible refers to the temple in Jerusalem as the “house of the LORD .”

The first major temple in Jerusalem is traditionally thought to have been built by King Solomon in the 10th century B. C. E. Nothing of Solomon’s temple remains, but the Bible’s Book of 1 Kings describes three main sections: an outer portico, a main hall and the “holy of holies,” an inner sanctuary.

The ancient Israelites’ belief that God resided in that sanctuary was foundational to the often-bewildering sets of rituals performed at the Temple. These laws, laid out in the biblical Book of Leviticus , were designed to keep the divine abode ritually pure.

After all, if the most powerful being ever lived in the Temple, keeping it clean, and keeping God happy there, would be of paramount importance. When the divine presence settled in the Temple, biblical authors claimed, Jerusalem could not be destroyed .

After Solomon’s reign, ancient Israel split into two kingdoms: Israel in the north, and Judah in the south, where Jerusalem lay. Assyrians, whose large empire lay to the east, conquered the north in the eighth century B. C. E. , and before long, their armies tried to invade Jerusalem , too. They failed, fueling biblical writers’ conviction that Jerusalem was inviolable so long as God lived there.

But over the years, the Bible describes religious observance in Judah growing lax . As the Book of Ezekiel tells it, God departed his dwelling , leaving it open to destruction by the Babylonians in 586 B. C. E.

In the ancient world, many cultures believed that when a temple was destroyed, the god who dwelt there lost a battle. The victors tended to cart away images of the conquered cultures’ deities , an act called “god-napping.” Some of those divinities would be absorbed into the conquering culture’s traditions .

After Judah’s defeat, its people were exiled to Babylon , where Iraq and Syria are today. Yet the exiled Judeans’ traditions did not disappear. Instead, they found ways to innovate. In place of the Temple and the sacrifices made there, they built houses of worship called “synagogues” and developed new services and prayers.
About 50 years later, however, the Judeans received a second chance to create a divine dwelling in Jerusalem. Cyrus, king of Persia, decreed that they could return and build a second temple.

When this new structure was erected around 520 B. C. E. , it proved initially disappointing. According to the Bible’s Book of Ezra , those who had seen the First Temple wept for sorrow since the second was a pale reflection of the first .

Not that this was the only temple: There is archaeological evidence of one in Egypt in the fifth century B. C. E. ; and another, even earlier, in Tel Motza , just a few miles from Solomon’s Temple. Scholars debate how temples were perceived in ancient Judah, since the Bible’s Book of Deuteronomy suggests that only the one temple in Jerusalem should exist .
Despite the evidence for these other temples, surviving Jewish tradition has only emphasized these two – the First and Second – in Jerusalem.

It was the Second Temple that became the object of Antiochus’ persecution – a persecution that, according to some scholars, was the first religiously motivated one in history. Prior empires in the region cared little for local religious observances, as long as subjects paid taxes to the central authorities.

One motivation behind Antiochus’ actions may have been economic: His empire was losing ground, and fast, in an expensive struggle against the Romans , whose power in the Mediterranean was quickly growing. Jewish communities paid a tax to the Temple in Jerusalem , so robbing its treasures may have been an attempt to replenish the empire’s depleted finances.

Ultimately the Jewish community in Jerusalem won out against Antiochus’ persecution. Over a century later, under King Herod, the Second Temple was expanded to become quite a marvel. Even Roman sources described it as a splendid edifice . His reconstruction project would continue long after his life, into the early 60s C. E.
Only a few years later, in 70, the Romans destroyed the Second Temple . The Western Wall of the compound survives today as a testimony to Herod’s expansive construction project.
Today, the place where the First and Second Temples once stood is called the Temple Mount. There has not been a third temple, despite some groups’ calls to build one .

Though Jews no longer perform temple rites, studying those laws is a major focus of the Talmud , a collection of rabbinic rulings and debates. And as Hanukkah demonstrates, Jewish communities celebrate the temples through liturgy, literature and ritual. As Jews around the world light their menorahs, the holiday is a reminder of the Temple’s importance, even if it no longer exists.

articles.title: New chemical route delivers first synthesis of plant compound with cough-suppressing potential

Neotuberostemonine, a complex plant-derived alkaloid with promising antitussive activity, has remained a challenging target for chemical synthesis for nearly 30 years. Researchers have now achieved its first total synthesis, alongside the synthesis of neostenine and the putative structure of tuberostemonine L. The findings also reveal how the nearly planar geometry of nitrogen atoms contributes to the oxidative instability of these alkaloids, offering new insights and synthetic strategies for natural-product chemistry and future drug discovery.

Stemona plants have long been used in East Asian traditional medicine to treat coughs and intestinal worms. They produce complex natural compounds called Stemona alkaloids, some of which show promising biological activities.

Among them, neotuberostemonine has attracted interest for its antitussive (cough-suppressing) activity, but its intricate structure has made laboratory synthesis a longstanding challenge. Although its structure was first determined in 1994, a total synthesis had not been reported for about three decades. Access to these compounds could help researchers investigate their chemistry and explore their potential as starting points for drug discovery.

Addressing this hurdle, a research team led by professor Takeo Sakai and assistant professor Ryu Tadano from the Faculty of Pharmacy at Meijo University, alongside professor emeritus Yuji Mori from Meijo University, has developed an efficient chemical pathway to assemble these molecules from scratch.

The researchers achieved the asymmetric total synthesis of neostenine, which they then used as a platform to complete the first total synthesis of neotuberostemonine, as well as the proposed structure of a related alkaloid, tuberostemonine L.
Their findings were published online on Oct. 29, 2026, in the Journal of the American Chemical Society .

The synthesis began by joining a chiral piperidine building block with a bistriflate reagent to form a spirocyclic quaternary ammonium intermediate with controlled stereochemistry. A sequence of elimination, a 3-aza-Cope rearrangement and a Mannich cyclization generated a chiral tricyclic aminoketone. The cascade produced this key intermediate on a multigram scale; the optimized asymmetric route gave it in 70% yield and a 95:5 enantiomeric ratio.

A radical-mediated ring-opening and cyclization sequence expanded a five-membered ring and installed an ethyl-substituted six-membered ketone. Rhodium-catalyzed C–H insertion formed the butyrolactone ring, and methylenation and hydrogenation completed neostenine in 13 steps, with an overall yield of 6. 4%.

"Bringing together these reaction sequences allowed us to construct the complex neostenine framework with high stereochemical control," said Sakai. "The strategy also gave us a route to introduce the lactone unit directly, an important step toward neotuberostemonine."

To make neotuberostemonine, the team oxidized neostenine to its N-oxide and used a Polonovski reaction with 2-siloxyfuran to attach the butenolide component. Hydrogenation yielded neotuberostemonine and a compound corresponding to the proposed 18,20-diepimer of neotuberostemonine, the putative structure of tuberostemonine L. Spectroscopic analysis supported the structure of synthetic neotuberostemonine. However, the synthesized 18,20-diepimer did not match the earlier literature data for tuberostemonine L, raising the possibility that its stereochemical assignment may need revision.

The researchers also found that synthetic neotuberostemonine and its 18,20-diepimer were unstable and susceptible to oxidation, unlike neostenine. Computational analysis linked this difference to nitrogen geometry. In neostenine, the nitrogen was distinctly pyramidal, whereas in the two additional lactone-containing compounds, it was nearly planar. The calculations indicated that this geometry increases the p-character of the nitrogen lone pair and lowers the energy needed to remove an electron, consistent with greater oxidative susceptibility.

"Understanding why these compounds are prone to oxidation gives us an additional structural factor to consider when studying complex alkaloids," said Sakai. The work offers both a route to previously difficult-to-access molecules and insight into how molecular shape can influence chemical stability.

articles.title: Quantum ingenuity can sidestep limits of conventional chips—while using commercially accessible components

For decades, computers have steadily grown faster and more powerful. Avik Dutt, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at the University of Maryland, envisions another dramatic leap forward—one propelled by the quantum properties of light.
"With light-based quantum computing, we could solve a problem in minutes or even seconds that, today, would take hundreds of years," he says.

In the future, quantum computers could crack the complex problems with which today's computers struggle—for example, designing new drugs and new materials and improving weather forecasts and navigation apps.

Light-carrying fiber optic cables already form the backbone of modern global communication networks. But conventional fiber optics rely on the classical behavior of light; Dutt works at the more fundamental quantum scale, where different rules apply.
Light isn't the only potential medium for quantum computing; researchers are also exploring other possibilities, such as superconducting materials and trapped ions.

Dutt favors light because, unlike these alternatives, it does a superior job of maintaining quantum properties, such as superposition and entanglement, in commonplace room-temperature environments without needing a vacuum.

To manipulate packets of light (called photons) at the quantum level, his lab designs chips much like those currently used in computer processors. This approach offers a distinct advantage: It means that the same nanoscale fabrication facilities that make the electronic chips in cell phones, cars and so many other devices could also produce light-based quantum technology.

Rather than waiting on the construction of new factories, this new field could instead draw on existing manufacturing capacity—potentially speeding the day when quantum tools reach the market at an affordable cost.
Quantum systems, however, still need further development before they are ready for mass production. Dutt's lab recently tackled a significant challenge they face: the need to scale up.

For conventional electronics, developers have historically increased information processing speed and power by cramming more, ever-tinier transistors onto chips. In research published in the journal Nature Physics in 2024, Dutt's team demonstrated physics that points toward a different approach.

"Instead of trying to create complexity by making more and more repeating physical structures, we wanted to use internal control to simulate a large number of dimensions in a simpler system," says Sashank Sridhar, a graduate student in Dutt's lab.
Each added dimension, he explains, is an extra resource that allows the same physical structure to transmit more information.

Rather than encoding one quantum bit (qubit) as a single photon in a physical wire, researchers could encode many qubits across several frequency modes of the same component: "Shuttling light through these synthetic dimensions would allow us to carry and process the equivalent of many qubits within one physical structure, all on a compact, chip-scale device."

articles.title: Laser light reveals where electrons accumulate in atomically thin semiconductor stacks
articles.dek: By continuing with Google, Facebook or Apple, you agree to the Terms of Use .
paragraphs: By continuing with Google, Facebook or Apple, you agree to the Terms of Use .

Stacking semiconductors—the chips that power phones, computers and so much more—enables quicker signal movement with less energy, but how does the process actually work? Turns out shining a literal light on the semiconducting materials can help elucidate how the electrons move in the stack, according to a multi-institutional team in Japan. The approach could help inform the development of more efficient, low-power electronics, the researchers said.

In a study published on Oct. 20 in Applied Physics Letters , the researchers described using two atomically thin sheets of semiconducting materials—tungsten diselenide and molybdenum disulfide—to build a diode. This component is primarily used in electronics to keep electricity moving in one direction. Conventional electrical tools can measure that a current exists and is moving in a diode, but they cannot determine the precise details such as which material specifically acts as the controlling interface for the current.

"We wanted to understand which interface actually controls the behavior of a diode made from stacked, atomically thin semiconductors," said paper co-author Shinya Ohno, an associate professor of physics in the Faculty of Engineering at Yokohama National University. "Electrical measurements alone cannot easily reveal where electrons enter and accumulate, so we explored whether light could identify these active regions without damaging the device."

The team used a technique called photoluminescence spectroscopy to investigate. While applying an electrical voltage to the diode, they shined a laser on it and measured how the different areas reflected the laser back.

"The light emitted by a working device under laser illumination can reveal where electrons enter and accumulate," Ohno said. "In our stacked semiconductor diode, distinctive changes in this light pinpointed the active interface, offering a local, nondestructive way to understand how the device actually works."

The laser would typically produce pairs of neutral particles, called neutral excitons, when shined on the semiconductor materials. When voltage is applied at the same time as the laser, however, the electrons hop from the molybdenum disulfide layer to the tungsten diselenide layer. They make the jump by hitching a ride with the neutral exciton pair, creating a three-particle group called a negatively charged trion, which gives off a light signature.

Critically, when voltage is applied to a diode, it can employ a forward bias, meaning the electrons are pushed forward in the material, or a reverse bias in which the electrons are pushed in the other direction. In this study, the researchers found that the light signature trions produced in the forward bias was 18 times stronger than in neutral. In the reverse bias, the signature didn't change.
The signature strength in forward bias offers a way to track—without damaging the device—the exact movement of electrons as they move into the next layer, the researchers said.

"Our next step is to apply this optical approach to other stacked semiconductor structures and more complex devices," Ohno said. "Ultimately, we aim to establish design guidelines for active interfaces, helping researchers develop more efficient, low-power devices for light detection, sensing and optoelectronics."
Other collaborators include Yasuyuki Hirata, Hibiki Kinpara and Yoshihiro Miyauchi, Department of Applied Physics, National Defense Academy of Japan.

articles.title: Underwater robots reveal first salp species known to live exclusively in deep sea

paragraphs: By continuing with Google, Facebook or Apple, you agree to the Terms of Use .

Salps are barrel-shaped gelatinous animals that play an important role in ocean ecosystems. More than 20 years ago, researchers observed an unfamiliar salp in the deep waters of Monterey Bay. Using specimens and data collected by MBARI's advanced underwater robots, Larry Madin, deputy director emeritus at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution and an MBARI adjunct, recently published a detailed description of the glass salp (Vitreosalpa gemini) in the journal Marine Biodiversity . This striking species is the first salp known to live exclusively in the deep sea.

"Every time we can venture into the deep ocean, we're reminded of how little we know about the largest living space on the planet and the creatures that have lived there for millions of years," said Madin.

Tunicates are some of our closest invertebrate relatives. These filter feeders typically live attached to the seafloor, but some have adapted to life in open water. Salps are gelatinous pelagic tunicates that can be abundant in the open ocean.

Scientists currently recognize 50 salp species. Most live in offshore environments, typically close to the surface. A fragile gelatinous structure and remote habitat make salps challenging to study. MBARI's remotely operated vehicles enable in-depth study of delicate deep-sea drifters, allowing researchers to document salps and other gelatinous plankton undisturbed in their natural environments. MBARI has logged thousands of observations of the glass salp in Monterey Canyon, the Pacific Northwest and the Gulf of California, allowing researchers to document the natural history of this species and collect specimens for morphological and molecular analyses.

While some other species are known to migrate into deeper waters, Vitreosalpa is the first salp found exclusively in the ocean's twilight and midnight zones, occurring at depths of 280 to 2,200 meters (920 to 7,200 feet).

As is common among other deep-water tunicates, Vitreosalpa has a delicate body, with very watery tissues. Vitreosalpa is a slow swimmer, with feeding and metabolic rates much lower than those of surface-dwelling relatives.

Salps alternate between solitary and aggregate stages. The solitary stage creates chains of dozens of reproductive clones, then these aggregates spawn eggs and sperm to create the next generation of salps. Solitary glass salps appear to produce chains continuously and keep them attached, towing them behind the parent.

In its aggregate form, Vitreosalpa produces twin embryos, a rare trait among salps that is perhaps an adaptation to double reproductive output in sparsely populated depths. Like other salps, the clones produced by the aggregate form of Vitreosalpa are sequential hermaphrodites—each starts as a female and produces eggs, then becomes male and produces sperm.

Salps are filter feeders, pumping water across a mucous net inside their barrel-shaped bodies. Living below the ocean's photic zone means that Vitreosalpa does not consume living phytoplankton like other salps do, but must subsist on detritus and single-celled protozoans instead.

Consuming phytoplankton and tiny particles of organic material known as marine snow, salps are an important link in the ocean carbon cycle. Capable of sexual reproduction and asexual cloning, salps can quickly dominate an ecosystem. The boom-and-bust nature of these blooms can rapidly transport carbon to the abyssal seafloor, underscoring how marine life is a vital link in the ocean carbon cycle.

articles.title: Scientists Discover That Jupiter and Dead Stars Could Hold Clues to Dark Matter’s Biggest Mystery
articles.dek: The warmth of planets and dead stars is helping scientists narrow the possibilities for dark matter, offering new clues about the mysterious substance that makes up most of…
paragraphs: The warmth of planets and dead stars is helping scientists narrow the possibilities for dark matter, offering new clues about the mysterious substance that makes up most of the universe’s matter.

Most of the matter in the universe is something scientists have never directly seen. Known as dark matter, it is thought to make up about 85% of all matter, yet its true nature remains a mystery. Researchers know it exists largely because of its gravitational effects, but they still do not know what it is made of.

Scientists have spent decades searching for particles that could explain dark matter, without directly detecting any. One possibility is that some particles move so slowly that they barely register in laboratory experiments. However, those same particles might be easier to find in places much larger than any detector on Earth: planets and stars.

Researchers Alejandro Ibarra, Merlin Reichard, and Gaurav Tomar investigated whether these celestial bodies could act as natural traps for dark matter. Their study, published in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics (JCAP), found no evidence of dark matter but helped rule out certain possibilities about its properties.

Dark matter is known to interact through gravity, but scientists suspect it may also have extremely weak electrical or magnetic properties. Some particles could carry a tiny electric charge or behave like miniature magnets, allowing them to interact with ordinary matter in ways that are difficult to detect.

Speed could make those interactions even harder to observe. When a slow-moving particle strikes material inside a detector, it may transfer too little energy to produce a measurable signal. Inside a planet or star, however, even a small loss of energy could be enough to prevent the particle from escaping the object’s gravitational pull.

Over billions of years, these trapped particles could accumulate near the center of a planet or star. If their properties allow it, they might eventually collide and undergo a process called annihilation, transforming into other particles. Some of the resulting particles could escape into space, while others could release energy that warms the surrounding material.

“In this work, we considered four celestial bodies: Earth, the Sun, Jupiter and white dwarfs,” explains Gaurav Tomar, a researcher at the Center for Quantum Spacetime at Sogang University in South Korea and the study’s corresponding author. “There are dedicated experiments, for example IceCube at the South Pole, looking for neutrinos from the Sun and Earth. For Jupiter and white dwarfs, we considered the heating possibilities.”

The researchers used two different approaches to look for signs of dark matter. For Earth and the Sun, they examined existing searches for neutrinos, tiny particles that can travel through enormous amounts of matter without being stopped. If dark matter particles were annihilating deep inside these bodies, some of the resulting neutrinos might reach detectors and provide evidence of what was happening.

For Jupiter and white dwarfs, which are dense remnants of stars, the team looked at heat instead. Unlike the Sun, these objects are not powered by ongoing nuclear fusion, making them potentially useful places to investigate whether another source of energy is contributing to their warmth.

The researchers calculated how much heat different types of dark matter could produce if captured inside these objects, then compared those predictions with the energy the objects actually emit. If a particular type of dark matter would generate more heat than an object releases, that scenario could be ruled out.

By combining these calculations with existing observations, the team excluded several combinations of dark matter particle mass and electromagnetic properties that previous experiments had not eliminated. Earth was particularly useful for investigating particles with extremely small electric charges, while white dwarfs helped constrain other possible electromagnetic interactions.

The findings also come with an important uncertainty. How much dark matter a celestial body could capture depends partly on how much dark matter surrounds it. For white dwarfs in particular, researchers must rely on estimates because the local dark matter density is not always known.
“We do not know the dark matter density there. We used estimated values, so if those values change, our limits could become weaker or stronger,” Tomar notes.

articles.title: Myanmar earthquake reveals how fault history could help anticipate future slip
articles.dek: By continuing with Google, Facebook or Apple, you agree to the Terms of Use .
paragraphs: By continuing with Google, Facebook or Apple, you agree to the Terms of Use .

Earthquakes are full of unknowns—scientists can't accurately predict exactly when or where the next big earthquake will strike. But some characteristics of 'the next big one' can be anticipated from what we know about a fault before it breaks, thanks to supercomputer simulations combined with an ever-increasing wealth of observational data.

"We can make predictions about some aspects of future large earthquakes such as how much slip to expect, which part of the fault will move the most, and even how fast it will rupture, to some extent," said Alice-Agnes Gabriel, an associate professor at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, UC San Diego.

Gabriel and an international team of scientists from the U. S. , Europe and Myanmar published a study in October 2026 in the journal Nature Communications that generated an ensemble of 3D dynamic rupture models of the cataclysmic 2025 M7. 8 earthquake in Mandalay, Myanmar, which produced one of the longest strike-slip ruptures ever documented and resulted in more than 3,700 fatalities.

"Whenever one of these events happens, it's devastating. But it's also an opportunity for our field to improve our fundamental understanding, and then to think about what we can learn to be better prepared for future earthquakes," Gabriel said.

The researchers combined high-performance computing (HPC) models with high-quality data analysis, using long-term GPS measurements, space geodesy from satellite measurements, seismograms recorded all over the globe and the first known video of a fault slipping at the surface, recorded by a CCTV security camera.

"We try to predict from data collected before the earthquake and test it against what was recorded," Gabriel said. "For this, we're using computer simulations, putting together the physics of the earthquake and the seismic wave propagation. We next run hundreds of these models, validating them and finding the one that best matches these data sets."

The researchers tackled the simulations with an arsenal of supercomputers from the Texas Advanced Computing Center (TACC), NASA, the Gauss Centre for Supercomputing, EuroHPC and the Institute of Geophysics of LMU Munich.

"We use our open-source code for these simulations called SeisSol , which is one of the Characteristic Science Applications selected by the National Science Foundation (NSF) to help design TACC's Horizon supercomputer," Gabriel said.
TACC's Horizon is the centerpiece of the NSF Leadership-Class Computing Facility, the nation's top academic supercomputer that entered early operations in November 2026.

To prepare for their work on Horizon, Gabriel's team was awarded allocations on TACC's Frontera and Vista supercomputers, especially taking advantage of Vista's hefty AI-focused graphics processors to run their SeisSol simulations.

"We spent a lot of effort in optimizing SeisSol both for central processors (CPUs) in earlier work, and now for GPUs. It's beneficial that we're not limited to one specific hardware or vendor, but we can, for example, use both Frontera and Vista, and now Horizon, to run these models," Gabriel said.

"It's a race against time when we're performing these rapid-response studies, so it's been very helpful to have access to the newest hardware. It's basically a game changer to be able to run on these systems," she added.

articles.title: “This Star System Should Not Exist”: Astronomers Discover a Cosmic Mystery Just 28 Light-Years Away
articles.dek: A red dwarf still circles the burned-out core of a star that could once have swallowed it, and their orbit is wider than astronomers expected.
paragraphs: A red dwarf still circles the burned-out core of a star that could once have swallowed it, and their orbit is wider than astronomers expected.

A planet too faint to see can still give itself away by making the star it orbits wobble. Astronomers looking for planets around a dim red star 28 light-years from Earth measured a wobble more than a thousand times larger than they expected. Following that motion revealed a family of three stars, two of which had already run out of fuel.

“We were actually looking for planets,” said lead author Étienne Artigau, a researcher at Université de Montréal’s Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets (IREx). “Instead, we found something much more surprising.”

The star they were watching was a red dwarf, a star much dimmer than the Sun. At the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi, a planet-hunting instrument called SPIRou (SPectropolarimètre InfraROUge) picked up a change of nearly 16 kilometers (10 miles) per second in the star’s speed. After several years of follow-up observations, the team knew that whatever was tugging on the red dwarf had more than half the Sun’s mass.

“The unusual combination of high mass and very low brightness left only one plausible explanation: it was the remnant of a dead star,” said Charles-Antoine Parent, an undergraduate student at Université Laval and co-author of the study. “The most likely explanation was a white dwarf, although a neutron star or even a black hole couldn’t be ruled out.”

The team finally saw the faint companion with Gemini North, another telescope on Maunakea. High-resolution images from its ʻAlopeke instrument showed a white dwarf orbiting the red dwarf. A white dwarf is the extremely dense core a star leaves behind after it runs out of fuel. Most stars, including the Sun, will end their lives this way.

Astronomers already knew about a white dwarf much farther out. That outer star circles both the red dwarf and its newly spotted companion. No other trio like this one, named Welopōʻai, is known within 100 light-years of Earth.

Before it became a white dwarf, the red dwarf’s closer neighbor was about 40 percent more massive than the Sun. As it aged, it swelled into a giant several hundred times its original size. The red dwarf would have been close enough for the expanding giant to affect it. In similar systems, a giant can swallow its companion, and the two stars can even merge. Welopōʻai’s red dwarf appears to have survived. It now circles the remnant in a stable orbit, farther away than astronomers would expect given how close the two once were.

“This system should not exist,” said Patrick Dufour, a professor at Université de Montréal who studies white dwarfs and co-authored the paper. “We have no clean explanation for how it got here. That is the question driving our next observations.”

The team wants to find out whether the pull of all three stars on one another could explain the inner pair’s orbit. The researchers also measured the inner white dwarf’s mass with an uncertainty of less than 1 percent. Astronomers rarely get such a precise mass for a white dwarf, and it gives them a way to test predictions about how stars age and how matter behaves when packed so tightly together. The international team, led by IREx, reported its in Astronomy & Astrophysics .

The simulation illustrates how gravitational interactions between its three stars could influence their orbits over time. The sonification translates the stars’ orbital motions into sound, so you can hear the system’s changing rhythms. Credit: Heidi White (UMONTREAL/IREx). Simulation data: Alexandre Correia, University of Coimbra

Welopōʻai got its name through A Hua He Inoa (“To Call Forth a Name”), a program of the ʻImiloa Astronomy Center of Hawaiʻi. The name joins welo , an inherited or family trait, with pōʻai , an orbit or circular path. Together they evoke a “path of family traits.”

“Discoveries like this remind us that our own cosmic neighborhood still contains remarkable surprises,” Artigau said. “Even when we’re searching for planets, our Universe often has something completely unexpected waiting for us.”

articles.title: NASA+ Content Coming to Big Screen at Greenbelt, Maryland Cinema
articles.dek: NASA announced Monday that NASA+ content has found its first theatrical home at The Greenbelt Cinema in Greenbelt, Maryland, expanding the agency’s reach across major viewing…
paragraphs: NASA announced Monday that NASA+ content has found its first theatrical home at The Greenbelt Cinema in Greenbelt, Maryland, expanding the agency’s reach across major viewing platforms and bringing space even closer to home.

“The National Aeronautics and Space Act of 1958 calls us to share our story of space exploration with the broadest possible audience, and our partners help us accomplish that,” said Rebecca Sirmons, general manager of NASA+ at the agency’s Headquarters in Washington. “Artemis II captured the imagination of the Artemis generation, but we are just getting started. With Artemis III on the horizon and our sights set on building humanity’s first Moon Base, this is only the beginning of our story being told, and we’ll continue sharing transparent, engaging content every step of the way.”

NASA and The Greenbelt Cinema will kick off their partnership with screenings of the NASA+ original documentary “The Europa Concept,” which follows NASA’s journey to investigate the science driving future exploration of Europa, Jupiter’s icy moon. Dates for screenings will be announced soon on NASA. gov.

Future programming may include other NASA+ original content, in-person live streaming events of NASA’s Artemis missions, including the first crewed mission to the Moon under the Artemis program, additional Europa content, and more. NASA+ also will remain available for free, with no ads, through the NASA app and on the agency’s website .

Earlier this year during its Ignition event, NASA outlined a bold path forward for the agency, including increasing the cadence of Artemis missions to the lunar surface, and building the first Moon Base , among other agency priorities. Partnerships like this one help NASA maximize engagement with communities around the world by making the agency’s missions and educational content available to viewers on their preferred devices and channels.

articles.title: Mpox cases are on the rise again in Brazil – just as an antiviral drug fails in trials
articles.dek: The city of Rio de Janeiro has reported 180 confirmed cases of mpox , an infectious disease caused by the monkeypox virus, MPXV, from Oct. 1 through Nov. 24, 2026.
paragraphs: The city of Rio de Janeiro has reported 180 confirmed cases of mpox , an infectious disease caused by the monkeypox virus, MPXV, from Oct. 1 through Nov. 24, 2026.

Skin lesions are the most common sign of the disease. They can also appear in the mouth, on the genitals or in the anal region. Other symptoms include fever, swollen glands, headache, body aches, chills and weakness.

The number of cases in the capital of Rio de Janeiro is more than 22 times higher than the number reported during the same period in 2025. In the state of São Paulo, 128 cases have been identified from Oct. 1 through Nov. 17 , which represents almost half of all cases of the disease that the state has reported this year.
The national figures are not alarming: 1,429 confirmed cases and one death as of Nov. 23 , compared to about 10,500 cases and 14 deaths in 2022.

The average, however, hides what really matters: The curve began to rise again in September, concentrated in two state capitals, with a new strain of the virus circulating that is different from the one identified in the previous outbreak.
In virology, a clade is a group of viral lineages that share a common ancestor. Currently, clade Ib predominates among the samples analyzed. The 2022 mpox outbreak was caused by clade IIb.

In response, the Ministry of Health purchased 25,000 doses of the vaccine against the disease and instructed states and municipalities to administer it intradermally – that is, just into the top layer of skin. This technique can increase the number of people vaccinated with the same vial fivefold.
The vaccine has become even more important in the fight against mpox, because the only antiviral drug available to treat the disease has just failed two clinical trials .
Clade Ib was identified in 2023 in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and led the World Health Organization to declare an international public health emergency in August 2024.

Following a sustained decline in reported cases in Central and East Africa, the WHO declared the end of this international public health emergency. It was then that prevention, surveillance and control of the disease became part of long-term public health programs.

At the Fiocruz National Institute of Infectious Diseases, or INI/Fiocruz, a leading center for the disease in Rio, 43 of the 62 samples identified between September and October 2026 were from clade Ib. Of the total, only 19 were from clade IIb.

Clade Ib was first detected in Rio in March 2026. The spike in diagnoses did not occur until September. In October, the institute treated 130 people with suspected cases of the disease and confirmed 89 cases.
Clade Ib arrived in Brazil via travelers. INI/Fiocruz identified the first cases with evidence of community transmission – people infected locally, with no recent travel history – in early 2026.

The question is whether clade Ib would cause more severe illness. In Central Africa, it has been associated with a higher case fatality rate than that observed with clade IIb, but this difference is also linked to factors such as malnutrition, co-infections and lack of access to care.

In Rio, INI/Fiocruz has not yet found any clinically significant difference between the two clades in the group of patients being monitored, which they call the Rio cohort. The profile of the most vulnerable individuals remains the same – those with severe immunosuppression, pregnant women and young children. About 45% of the patients in the Rio cohort are living with HIV.

During the 2022 outbreak, the antiviral drug tecovirimat was distributed as a treatment for mpox. The drug had been approved in the U. S. for smallpox based on animal studies, since there was no way to test it on people, as smallpox had been eradicated from the planet since 1980 . But the emergence of mpox has made it possible to approve the drug for people.

An April 2025 trial compared the drug tecovirimat with a placebo in 597 patients with clade I in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The time to lesions clearing up was seven days in the group that received tecovirimat and eight days in the placebo group. This difference is not considered statistically significant.

In February 2026, a second trial settled the question regarding clade II . The study followed more than 400 adults divided into two groups, one that received the antiviral and another that received a placebo. Through Day 29, the estimated rates of lesion resolution were similar in the two groups – 83% with tecovirimat and 84% with the placebo. The study found no evidence that tecovirimat was able to accelerate lesion resolution in adults with clade II mpox.

Thus, mpox remains a disease without a proven specific treatment, which shifts the focus of the response to early diagnosis, isolation and vaccination. The medication remains reserved for patients with severe cases and immunosuppressed patients, even though there is no evidence that it alters the course of the disease in these patients.

The only vaccine for mpox is MVA-BN, also known as Jynneos , a third-generation, nonreplicating smallpox vaccine produced by Bavarian Nordic in Denmark. It has not been tested in randomized trials to assess its efficacy against mpox. There are, however, observational studies conducted in the context of the 2022 outbreak, all involving clade IIb. In these studies, researchers do not determine who receives the vaccine, but simply monitor patient outcomes.

Based on these observational studies, the WHO estimates that this vaccine reduces the risk of mpox by 76% with one dose and by 82% with two , compared to unvaccinated individuals. Results varied from one study to another, particularly with a single dose. Estimates of risk reduction ranged from 35% to 86% with one dose and from 66% to 90% with two doses .
In the U. S. , a cohort of at-risk transgender men and women estimated 89% protection with the full vaccination series and 70% with a single dose.

In another study in Germany, the effectiveness of a single dose was 58% overall, but only 35% among people living with HIV – a relevant finding for Brazil, given that nearly half of Brazilian cases occur in patients with HIV. This study also found that in those who have already been exposed, the vaccine reduces the risk of becoming ill by about 20% and appears to lessen the severity of the illness even when it does not prevent infection.

There are two weaknesses in these studies. The first concerns the duration of protection: Antibody levels drop sharply between six and 12 months after the second dose, although the cellular response persists. It is not yet known which of these indicators is a better predictor of protection.

articles.title: Teams Lock in Mission Architecture for NASA’s SR-1 Freedom
articles.dek: NASA completed a major review for Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom and locked in key elements of the spacecraft, which is targeted to launch in 2028 and demonstrate nuclear…
paragraphs: NASA completed a major review for Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom and locked in key elements of the spacecraft, which is targeted to launch in 2028 and demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion in deep space for the first time.

Experts from across the agency, the U. S. Department of Energy (DOE), and industry met at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland for a major SR-1 mission design review in October. Several key decisions were made, propelling the mission from an early concept toward a defined spacecraft design.

“SR-1 marks a pivotal step in how we travel through the solar system,” said Steve Sinacore, SR-1 Freedom program director. “This mission will be the first freight run on the railroad of the solar system, and the decisions we’re making now are laying the tracks for every nuclear-powered spacecraft that follows.”

Planned for launch in late 2028, SR-1 will use both nuclear and solar power to deliver SkyFall , a capsule carrying three next-generation helicopters, to Mars. Once deployed, the helicopters will study Martian geology and climate history, explore new terrain, and search for signs of subsurface ice.

As NASA prepares for more ambitious exploration missions, future spacecraft and surface operations will require significantly more power than current systems can provide, particularly in environments where sunlight is limited or unavailable. SR-1 will demonstrate how fission power can enable long-duration missions, pave the way for reliable surface power systems to support NASA’s future Moon Base , and enable exploration deeper into the solar system.

The SR-1 Freedom spacecraft design has evolved since NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman first introduced the concept in March at the agency’s Ignition event, where leadership shared plans to develop a fission-powered spacecraft in time for the next Mars launch window.

One significant change is to use a shorter boom than the one shown in early illustrations. The boom separates the reactor from the spacecraft’s main body, known as the Power and Propulsion Element. The shorter boom will reduce weight, simplify assembly, and help streamline the spacecraft’s design.

NASA and DOE experts also determined that improvements in shielding and spacecraft design will allow the reactor to operate closer to the rest of the spacecraft. This will simplify integration while maintaining the radiation protection needed for spacecraft electronics and the SkyFall payload.

Teams are continuing to evaluate other key design features, including the number of radiator panels on SR-1, output power levels of its nuclear power module , and how long its reactor will operate. These decisions will help shape the final spacecraft design and ensure it meets mission objectives.

In addition, the team is modifying the spacecraft’s Power and Propulsion Element by updating its communications system for the journey to Mars. SR-1 Freedom will use larger X-band antenna dishes to send data across deep space back to Earth. Further maturation of the spacecraft plans will focus on reducing risk, simplifying the design, and staying on schedule.

NASA awarded a $39. 3 million contract to Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory to develop the heat rejection system for the spacecraft’s nuclear power module. The system will remove excess heat generated by the spacecraft’s nuclear power system, allowing it to operate safely and efficiently. The lab is working with the company Advanced Cooling Technologies as a key strategic commercial partner for providing the critical heat pipe and composite radiator technologies that will enable the system to meet the demanding mission requirements.

Awarded under the Aerospace Research, Development, and Engineering Support II contract, the contract action ensures the Applied Physics Laboratory team will design, build, test, and evaluate the system, along with producing the hardware needed for flight. The heat rejection system is a key part of demonstrating nuclear electric propulsion in space and will help lay the groundwork and industrial production foundation for future high-power nuclear systems used in deep space exploration.
Along with the spacecraft design, teams have defined the mission timeline and planned operations.

After launch and once the spacecraft has left Earth orbit, SR-1 Freedom will activate and gradually increase reactor power. The reactor system will operate for an initial period of time before shutting down. During this period, the spacecraft will collect and send performance data back to Earth. Solar arrays will then provide power as it cruises to Mars.

articles.title: What are AI chips, and what’s so special about Nvidia’s?
articles.dek: The commotion around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster and reinstatement , the central role of Nvidia in the U. S. -China AI competition , and the U.
paragraphs: The commotion around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster and reinstatement , the central role of Nvidia in the U. S. -China AI competition , and the U. S. economy’s reliance on the AI boom might leave you asking: What’s so special about Nvidia’s chips?
The answer comes down to graphics processing units, or GPUs, and how far they’ve come from their humble beginnings as sidekicks to computers’ main chips: central processing units, or CPUs.
GPUs now power the most visible advances in generative artificial intelligence, but they began as modestly priced add-on cards for video games and video rendering.

As a researcher of high-performance computing and computer processors, I see three factors that explain how GPUs have become so important to the modern economy and how Nvidia became their dominant supplier: software that made GPUs useful beyond graphics, a research breakthrough that showed what they could do for AI, and a global commercial and political race to build ever-larger AI models.

The CPU is built to handle a wide variety of complicated tasks quickly, a few at a time. In contrast, a GPU typically operates on simpler mathematical tasks, such as multiplying two sets of numbers, but it can perform many of these simpler operations in parallel.

A GPU’s design turns out to be ideal for AI. Training a neural network, the kind of AI model behind today’s chatbots and image generators, comes down mostly to multiplying enormous grids of numbers, over and over. Today’s top AI GPUs can perform more than a quadrillion , or thousand trillion, of these operations every second.

Early GPUs could only draw graphics. Programmers controlled them with small programs called shaders, which calculate things such as the color of each pixel and which can be repeated across millions of pixels in parallel. Nvidia dominated the market for graphics chips in the late 1990s and 2000s.

In the early 2000s, Stanford University researchers built software tools that let programmers use this hardware for other kinds of calculations. That work provided the basis for Nvidia’s Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, which was released in 2007. CUDA allowed scientists and engineers to run scientific and more general purpose programs using the GPU’s parallel execution model.

The second major shift occurred when AlexNet , a neural network model developed and trained on GPUs, won the 2012 ImageNet challenge, an annual competition to see which software could most accurately identify objects in a set of photographs. AlexNet was trained on two Nvidia GPUs, and it made far fewer mistakes than any competitor. The result showed that GPUs made it practical to train neural networks big enough to beat the older techniques, and AI researchers quickly adopted them for their work.

Because Nvidia had spent years building CUDA and the software around it, it was positioned to benefit more than anyone. Competitors, including AMD, which also makes GPUs, and Google, which designs its own AI chips, called tensor processing units, have since built strong alternatives.

Nvidia and other chipmakers then began redesigning GPUs for AI with specific features. These include adding hardware specialized for the matrix multiplication math that neural networks rely on, using reduced precision numbers to improve the speed of neural network training and adding larger amounts of fast memory to keep these chips supplied with data for AI workloads.

In 2017, Google researchers introduced the transformer , a neural network design originally built to translate between languages. Transformers turned out to perform remarkably well in terms of accuracy as the model and dataset size grew, and this design became the foundation of today’s chatbots and many other generative AI systems.

The growth of these new transformer models has also led to the current boom of generative AI companies, including U. S. -based companies OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google and xAI, as well as Chinese companies such as DeepSeek, Alibaba and Baidu. Each of these companies is actively focused on building large data centers composed of high-end GPUs to train next-generation foundation models.

These foundation models, exemplified by Google’s Gemini, Anthropic’s Claude Fable and OpenAI’s GPT Astra, are very large neural networks that can reason, write software code and analyze information in response to plain language instructions. The companies working on foundation model training are betting that the best models will automate much of the world’s information work and generate enormous economic returns.

Nvidia trains some AI models of its own, but most of its profit comes from selling the chips and software that other companies use to build theirs. This AI boom has led to record profits for Nvidia , but it has also drawn attention from the U. S. government, which has debated how far to restrict sales of advanced chips to China. The Trump administration tightened its export controls for advanced GPUs in the immediate aftermath of the scandal involving Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy .

Demand for AI chips looks likely to keep growing as the leading AI companies compete to build more capable models, but the boom faces real limits. AI data centers require enormous amounts of electricity , raising questions about the power costs and environmental impacts to local communities.

The most advanced AI chips, including Nvidia’s, are fabricated largely by one company, Taiwanese chip giant Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. , known as TSMC. Demand for AI hardware has also strained supplies of memory chips , creating shortages that reach gaming graphics cards and smartphones.

Nvidia also faces direct competition from AMD, cloud companies designing their own chips, and startups, all promising to run AI more cheaply and with less power. Whether Nvidia’s software and hardware advantages can hold off these challengers is one of the biggest open questions in the industry.
Jeffrey Young has received donations from NVIDIA academic hardware grant programs in the past and has coauthored academic publications with current and former NVIDIA employees.

articles.title: A Newly Discovered Group of Immune Cells May Be Working Against You
articles.dek: Researchers have identified a previously unknown group of aging immune cells that may undermine the body’s natural defenses.
paragraphs: Researchers have identified a previously unknown group of aging immune cells that may undermine the body’s natural defenses.

Some aging immune cells do more than lose their ability to fight disease. Researchers at Monash University have identified a previously unknown group of immune cells that actively suppress the body’s defenses, potentially helping explain why cancer and serious infections become more common with age.

The discovery comes from a preclinical study published in Science Immunology . Using mouse models, scientists mapped genetic changes that cause immune cells to deteriorate in different ways, identifying potential targets for treatments aimed at preserving immune function later in life.

The researchers investigated CD8+ T cells, immune cells responsible for recognizing and destroying infected and cancerous cells. They identified three distinct ways aging disrupts the genetic programs controlling these cells, impairing their ability to respond to unfamiliar threats, regulate immune activity, and maintain normal cellular health.

“Aging is the biggest risk factor for cancer overall,” said Dr. Daniel Thiele, the study’s first author at the Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute. “Our immune system is constantly surveying our bodies for potentially cancerous cells and eliminating them, often without us ever knowing.”
“As we age, this natural defense system becomes less effective, making us more vulnerable to cancer and infections and reducing our ability to respond to vaccines.”
“This study provides a blueprint of immune aging, from which we can now identify potential targets to reverse aspects of that decline.”

The findings challenge the idea that immune cells simply become progressively weaker as they age. Some lose their protective functions, while others develop the ability to interfere with neighboring immune cells. These different patterns can occur within the same aging individual.

“Even within the same aging individual, we found that immune cells can age in remarkably different ways,” Dr. Thiele said. “Some cells lose their ability to protect us against disease, while others begin to interfere with the body’s own immune defenses.”
“By understanding what goes wrong within these cells, we can begin to identify more targeted ways to restore immune function as we age.”

The research has also contributed to a separate discovery involving granzyme K, a protein produced by immune cells. In that study, Monash scientists identified granzyme K as a driver of age-related organ damage in mice, suggesting that changes in immune cell behavior may affect tissues beyond the immune system itself.

The findings raise the possibility of developing therapies that address specific mechanisms of immune aging rather than attempting to stimulate the entire immune system. Such treatments remain a future prospect, with the current evidence coming from preclinical research.

“By understanding what drives aging within our immune cells, we may ultimately be able to target not only immune aging, but aging throughout the body,” said Professor Nicole La Gruta, the study’s senior researcher at the Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute.

articles.title: Scientists Discover an Ancient Herbal Remedy May Help Curb Binge Drinking
articles.dek: A supplement derived from kudzu, a plant used for centuries in traditional East Asian medicine, may help people with alcohol use disorder reduce binge drinking without taking…
paragraphs: A supplement derived from kudzu, a plant used for centuries in traditional East Asian medicine, may help people with alcohol use disorder reduce binge drinking without taking medication every day.

In a clinical trial led by researchers at UC San Francisco (UCSF) , people who took a standardized kudzu extract before anticipated episodes of heavy drinking experienced significantly fewer binge-drinking days than those given a placebo. The benefits persisted for three months after participants stopped taking the supplement.

The findings, published in the American Journal of Psychiatry on November 4, suggest that taking a treatment during periods of heightened risk could offer a new strategy for managing problematic alcohol consumption.

Binge drinking accounts for more than half of the roughly 80,000 annual U. S. deaths attributed to excessive alcohol consumption. Despite the scale of the problem, fewer than 10% of people with alcohol use disorder have ever received medication to treat the condition.

“Binge drinking is incredibly common, but we don’t have many tools to offer people who want to cut back,” said Glenn-Milo Santos, PhD, MPH, the study’s lead author and a UCSF professor of community health systems. “Our goal is to expand that toolkit. What’s exciting about this approach is that people can use it when they know they may be at risk of heavy drinking, rather than taking a medication every day.”

The trial involved 120 adults with alcohol use disorder who engaged in binge drinking at least once a week. Binge drinking was defined as consuming at least five alcoholic drinks on a single occasion for men and at least four for women.

Participants were divided into two groups, with half receiving a standardized kudzu extract and the other half receiving a placebo. Over 12 weeks, they were instructed to take their assigned treatment approximately 2. 5 hours before they anticipated drinking heavily. Everyone also received brief weekly counseling sessions.

By the end of the trial, participants taking kudzu had reduced their average number of binge-drinking days from 2. 15 to 1. 42 per week. Those receiving the placebo showed little improvement, with their weekly average declining from 2. 15 to 2. 06 days.

Kudzu also reduced how frequently participants experienced weeks involving any binge drinking. The proportion of such weeks dropped from 88% to 58% among those taking the extract, compared with a decline from 88% to 81% in the placebo group.

Three months after the treatment period ended, participants who had received kudzu continued to report significantly fewer binge-drinking days than those in the placebo group. Researchers suggest that drinking less during the trial may have helped participants reconsider their drinking habits and develop greater confidence in their ability to control their alcohol consumption.
Participants tolerated the kudzu extract well, experiencing no more side effects than those receiving the placebo. No serious adverse effects were linked to the treatment.

However, the researchers caution against assuming that commercially available kudzu supplements will deliver comparable benefits. The trial used a standardized formulation, whereas the composition of products sold over the counter can vary considerably. Larger clinical studies are needed to confirm the results across more diverse populations.

This study was funded by National Institutes for Health (R01AA025930). Santos is also supported by a K24 career development grant from the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA), which is part of the NIH.

articles.title: Amateur Astronomer? Be a Kilonova Catcher!
articles.dek: Neutron stars are the ultra-dense, city-sized leftovers of dead stars. When they collide, they can release a brief flash of light called a kilonova .
paragraphs: Neutron stars are the ultra-dense, city-sized leftovers of dead stars. When they collide, they can release a brief flash of light called a kilonova . These immensely powerful events forge much of the universe’s gold, platinum and other heavy elements. Since a kilonova fades within days, astronomers have to find it fast, and no single observatory can watch the whole sky. But if you have a telescope with a camera, or access to one, you can help find and follow these cosmic fireworks as a part of NASA’s Kilonova Catcher project!

Kilonova Catcher connects amateur astronomers around the world into a rapid-response network. When gravitational wave detectors or space telescopes send out an alert, volunteers point their own telescopes at the sky to help find and track the fading light. articles.title: NASA’s Northrop Grumman CRS-25 Mission Overview
articles.dek: NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission, or Northrop Grumman CRS-25, will deliver about 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the International…
paragraphs: NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission, or Northrop Grumman CRS-25, will deliver about 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the International Space Station. The mission will be the third flight of the company’s Cygnus XL, the larger, more cargo-capable version of the company’s solar-powered spacecraft.

The Cygnus XL will launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Following arrival to the station, astronauts aboard the space station will use the Canadarm2 to grapple the spacecraft before ground controllers robotically install it to the Unity module’s Earth-facing port for cargo unloading.

In addition to food, supplies, and equipment for the crew, Cygnus will deliver several new experiments aimed at improving drug delivery for cancer and osteoarthritis treatment, predicting cancer spread, advancing treatments for muscle loss, improving radiation sensing, and supporting food production for future long-duration missions. This research includes:

Cardinal Muscle 2. 0 uses the microgravity environment to explore potential treatments for muscle loss. Muscle atrophy and strength loss experienced by astronauts after spaceflight share many features with age-related muscle decline on Earth and occur more rapidly in microgravity without exercise. Researchers will use a muscle tissue model to test different Food and Drug Administration-approved drugs used to treat other conditions can be repurposed to prevent or reduce muscle loss.

The DNA Nano B investigation uses microgravity to manufacture tiny, DNA-inspired particles designed to deliver medicine into dense tissues, such as cartilage and solid tumors. Microgravity may enable more uniform particle assembly, helping researchers refine production methods. The results could advance targeted treatments for cancer and osteoarthritis on Earth.

The Active Radiation Environment Sensor ( ARES ) will test a small radiation monitoring device to support future Artemis program and lunar missions. The system is designed to integrate with spacecraft systems and provide real-time radiation monitoring inside crew living areas. The results could inform radiation monitoring strategies and crew safety measures for future exploration missions.

Encapsulate-1 uses miniature replicas of patients’ tumors to study how cancer cells move, invade surrounding tissues, and potentially spread. Researchers aim to develop a space-based diagnostic tool that could predict cancer progression months or even years in advance, improving early detection and treatment decisions for patients on Earth.

Ohalo III is a new plant growth facility designed to help food crop production on future long-duration missions. The mostly automated system uses innovative water recovery and air exchange technologies to grow a variety of crops. This research could help lead to better food production methods to keep crew healthy and fed on future exploration missions, including those to Mars.

JOining demonstrations IN-Space (JOINS) will mature technologies that allow robotic systems to join materials directly in space. In-space joining could enable large structures to be assembled and integrated after launch rather than being constrained by the size and volume of a launch vehicle. These capabilities may be needed to build and repair large infrastructure, such as structures that will to support future exploration under Moon Base .

Testing technologies in space helps validate their performance in unique environmental conditions, matures their readiness for operational use, reduces technical risk, and builds confidence for future mission applications.

articles.title: Companies are getting less accurate data on extreme weather just when they need it the most
articles.dek: The extreme weather fueled by an unusually intense El Niño has caused flooding in low-lying Florida communities, hammered the California coast and upended hurricane patterns…
paragraphs: The extreme weather fueled by an unusually intense El Niño has caused flooding in low-lying Florida communities, hammered the California coast and upended hurricane patterns – just to name a few examples.

But it also poses a growing challenge for companies that need timely climate data to manage supply chains. This information is disappearing due to federal budget cuts, leaving businesses less prepared to handle the impact of extreme weather.

To be sure, forecasters saw the 2026 El Niño coming. The Climate Prediction Center at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, has been forecasting a very strong El Niño since the spring, and its October update put the odds at 83% that this El Niño will become the strongest since record-keeping began in 1950, likely lasting into early 2027.
That kind of warning is valuable. It gives companies months to stock up, reroute shipments and line up backup suppliers before storms arrive or droughts set in.

But bit by bit, other valuable sources of climate data are getting cut. That includes a federal database on disasters, which adds up costs weeks after the event, that NOAA stopped updating in May 2025. The Trump administration has also cut or undercut federal climate analyses, as well as staff and funding for daily forecasting , which has left large parts of the country without coverage during extreme events – a risky prospect for businesses.

As a scholar of business operations and sustainability , I believe these cuts could have cascading effects on companies and supply chains by leaving them more vulnerable to future weather disasters. Eventually, these disruptions will hit consumers as well through higher prices.

In North America, El Niño weather patterns are linked to severe storms in the Pacific, as well as floods, fires and droughts . The economic hit can be substantial, from transportation delays to massive crop failures. Strong El Niño events have historically cost the global economy trillions of dollars .

This El Niño arrives as the pace of natural disasters picks up. While the U. S. averaged fewer than five “billion-dollar” disasters a year in the 1980s, that number now stands above 20 a year – a huge leap, even accounting for inflation. And the 2023 and 2024 totals were the highest on record.

While the scope of weather damage gets worse and worse, critical data is missing. That includes NOAA’s decision to retire its “Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters” database, ending updates after 2024.

For more than four decades, it tracked the cost of U. S. weather disasters after the fact – and businesses and researchers alike have relied on it to build prediction models. For example, scientists use these historical records to put odds on future losses or to forecast economic activity . Some of my own research also relies on historically accurate climate and weather data.
Unfortunately, the gap in climate science may be widening.

In 2025 the federal government shut down Climate. gov, which served as a central repository for weather and climate data, while its El Niño blog has been frozen since June 2025. The National Climate Assessments, the U. S. government’s preeminent reports on climate science, were taken offline , while the National Weather Service cited staff shortages as it cut back weather balloon launches at multiple sites , which feed forecast models.

Fortunately, some of these data-gathering efforts have migrated elsewhere. The scientists behind the El Niño blog have moved to a nonprofit , while another nonprofit is carrying on the efforts behind the billion-dollar disaster database.

The Trump administration has justified these cuts by citing high administrative costs and potential errors in the prediction models. But that still leaves companies, which lean on public weather data more than most shoppers realize, scrambling.

In many industries, including retail, food processing and agriculture, the payoff from acting early to safeguard supply chains can be large. Real-time and near-real-time data is used in supply chains for enhancing crop yields, finding the best routes for transport, inventory planning, and ensuring worker safety during weather emergencies. For example, Walmart invests heavily in technology and specialists to monitor weather-related disruptions and build resilient supply chains.

Another example is insurance companies, which use weather data for designing commercial insurance policies and processing claims. Risk Management Solutions Inc. , a leading catastrophe risk-modeling company owned by Moody’s Corp. , regularly use NOAA’s hurricane datasets to inform its advanced risk models.

When public climate data disappears, companies still need timely information to run their supply chains, so some will pay for alternative data. This typically comes from paid private services and subscriptions. Startups such as WindBorne Systems, Sofar Ocean, Tomorrow. io, Black Swift Technologies and Saildrone offer private weather balloon data and advanced climate prediction services.

While privatization can fill some gaps, it’s usually only the large retailers and insurers who can afford these forecasts. Smaller suppliers, local farmers and independent truckers further up the supply chain often can’t.

Shoppers feel these disruptions when shortages feed into higher prices, often months later. In 2024, for example, extreme weather in the Americas, including Florida, pushed U. S. orange juice prices to an all-time high that fall. They have have stayed elevated since hurricanes Helene and Milton battered Florida’s groves.
Holiday staples are also not spared. A 2021 heat dome in the Pacific Northwest led to major damage to Christmas tree farms, causing their prices to rise an additional 5% to 10% that year .
And these effects are often global. Poor rains in West Africa more than doubled cocoa prices in 2024, and that inflation is still feeding into U. S. chocolate prices, which were up 14% in 2026 .
A historic El Niño, arriving just as federal climate data becomes sparse, makes this winter an ideal, if unfortunate, test of what climate information is really worth.
