articles.title: Scientists Discover the Human Ear May Work Very Differently Than We Thought
articles.dek: New research challenges a long-standing theory of how the inner ear detects sound, revealing a more complex process than previously understood.
paragraphs: New research challenges a long-standing theory of how the inner ear detects sound, revealing a more complex process than previously understood.

Scientists have discovered that low-frequency sounds can produce nearly simultaneous vibrations across widely separated regions of the inner ear. The finding, observed in guinea pigs, challenges a long-standing model of how hearing works and could influence the development of more advanced cochlear implants.

For decades, scientists have understood the cochlea, the spiral-shaped structure inside the inner ear, as a frequency map. Different sounds activate different locations along its membrane, much like individual piano keys correspond to specific notes. High frequencies stimulate one end, while low frequencies primarily activate the other. This arrangement, known as the “place code,” has helped explain how the ear distinguishes sounds and forms a foundation of modern cochlear implant technology.

The traditional model dates back to research by Georg von Békésy, who received the 1961 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for demonstrating how different sound frequencies stimulate distinct regions of the cochlea. However, the new study, published in Science Advances , suggests that this location-based explanation does not fully account for how the inner ear processes low-frequency sounds.

To investigate, researchers used optical coherence tomography (OCT), an imaging technology (co-invented by OHSU physician-scientist David Huang) widely used in eye examinations. Combined with advanced signal processing to reduce background noise, the technique allowed scientists to detect extremely small vibrations at multiple locations inside the guinea pig cochlea.

The measurements showed that low-frequency sounds produced similar vibrations across distant regions, often with synchronized motion. Rather than disproving the cochlea’s frequency map, the findings indicate that additional mechanisms may contribute to how low-frequency information is represented and interpreted. The results build on earlier research published in 2022 that identified unexpected patterns of low-frequency responses.

Understanding low-frequency hearing is particularly important for interpreting complex sounds, including speech. These vibrations are difficult to measure experimentally, and people with hearing loss often struggle to understand conversations when background noise is present.

“When you bring in low-frequency background noise, it’s a very challenging environment for people with hearing loss,” said George Burwood, Ph. D. , the study’s lead author and a research instructor at Oregon Health & Science University (OHSU). “Also, the place code paradigm limits the interpretation of how mammals evolved to detect extremely complex signals, especially speech.”

Current cochlear implants use electrodes to electrically stimulate different regions of the cochlea according to sound frequency. The new findings suggest that reproducing more of the natural cochlea’s complex vibration patterns might improve how these devices convey sound information.

“Cochlear implants are geared to take advantage of a place code,” Burwood said. “Our study suggests the optimal pattern of stimulation by electrodes in a cochlear implant may be more complex than just where and how intensely it’s being stimulated.”

The findings also raise questions about how the auditory system separates frequencies when vibrations are distributed across multiple cochlear locations. Researchers suspect the brain may use information beyond the position of stimulation to distinguish certain sounds.

“This discovery advances our basic understanding in how hearing works,” said Larry Trussell, Ph. D. , director of the Oregon Hearing Research Center at OHSU. “The brain appears to have mechanisms that are able to differentiate frequencies without having a map or place code.”
The research at OHSU was supported by the National Institutes of Health through award R01DC00141-44.

All research involving animal subjects at OHSU must be reviewed and approved by the university’s Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) . The IACUC’s priority is to ensure the health and safety of animal research subjects. The IACUC also reviews procedures to ensure the health and safety of the people who work with the animals. No live animal work may be conducted at OHSU without IACUC approval.

articles.title: Researchers Have Discovered a Previously Unknown Crystal Form of Silver
articles.dek: Researchers have discovered a previously unknown crystal structure of silver that exhibits unusually high chemical reactivity.
paragraphs: Researchers have discovered a previously unknown crystal structure of silver that exhibits unusually high chemical reactivity.

Silver can take on an extraordinarily rare atomic structure that makes it far more chemically reactive than its familiar form. Researchers at Hokkaido University have discovered a previously unknown crystal arrangement in which silver atoms form a simple cubic pattern, a structure previously documented in only one other element.

The findings, published in Nano Letters , emerged when scientists used an electron beam to break down silver iodide and observed the resulting silver crystals at the atomic scale. Unlike ordinary silver, the newly formed crystals began converting into silver oxide within approximately 100 seconds, demonstrating how dramatically atomic arrangement can influence a material’s chemical behavior.

Most silver crystallizes in a structure known as face-centered cubic, in which atoms occupy the eight corners and the center of each face of a repeating cube. This tightly packed arrangement is also found in common metals such as gold, copper, and aluminum.

The newly discovered silver instead formed a simple cubic structure, with atoms occupying only the corners of each repeating cube. This arrangement is exceptionally uncommon in pure elements. Before this discovery, the only known elemental example was radioactive polonium, whose simple cubic structure was identified in 1966.

“It was surprising to find that such a low-density structure could form in a pure metal crystal,” says first author Dr. Masaya Sakakibara. “We expected silver nanoparticles to form when silver iodide decomposes under electron beam irradiation, but we didn’t expect them to adopt a simple cubic structure.”

The researchers created and examined the silver using a transmission electron microscope (TEM), which employs electrons with wavelengths shorter than those of visible light to resolve structures down to individual atoms. The electron beam served two purposes: it triggered the decomposition of silver iodide and allowed the scientists to watch the resulting silver atoms organize into crystals.

The nanoscale conditions were essential to the discovery. At dimensions of just a few billionths of a meter, materials can temporarily adopt crystal structures that would be unstable in larger samples. Such arrangements can produce physical and chemical properties that differ substantially from those of the same element in its conventional form.

Experiments conducted under high vacuum revealed a striking difference between the two silver structures. Conventional face-centered cubic silver remained stable, while the simple cubic crystals gradually oxidized, forming silver oxide. The rapid transformation provided direct evidence of the new structure’s unusually high chemical reactivity.
“Within 100 seconds of its formation, it began to transform into silver oxide,” adds Sakakibara.
The researchers believe their technique could provide a way to discover other previously unknown crystal structures and investigate the properties they produce.

“This is a new approach to discovering previously unknown crystal structures, which could also help us develop materials with novel properties in the future,” says Professor Yuki Kimura, co-author of the study and head of the Low Temperature Nanomaterial Science Laboratory at Hokkaido University.
“Going forward, we will continue investigating the physical and chemical properties of simple cubic silver in greater detail and extend this approach to other elements and compounds.”

articles.title: NASA’s Titan-Bound Dragonfly Rotorcraft Gets Its Eyes
articles.dek: Science instruments for NASA’s Dragonfly are starting to arrive at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland, where the car-sized rotorcraft is…
paragraphs: Science instruments for NASA’s Dragonfly are starting to arrive at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland, where the car-sized rotorcraft is coming together for its mission to explore Saturn’s largest moon, Titan.

First to check in: DragonCam, which consists of seven cameras designed to characterize Titan ’s surface at multiple scales during flight and while on the ground. By mid-November, all seven cameras developed and built by Malin Space Science Systems had been installed in their insulated housings, tested, and integrated into the rotorcraft. Each camera will look out at Titan through a window in a foam enclosure that insulates the cameras and Dragonfly’s interior from Titan’s cryogenic environment, where ambient temperatures reach minus 290 degrees Fahrenheit.

A configurable LED array, built at APL and spanning the light spectrum from the infrared to the ultraviolet, provides information about the color of surface materials at the sampling site and helps scientists make inferences about their composition. During Titan’s long night, which spans nearly eight Earth days, these observations also may allow DragonCam to identify organic molecules that fluoresce under ultraviolet light. The LED illumination also allows us to see Titan as human eyes would.

“One of the most exciting things about Dragonfly is that we’ll be able to see Titan from perspectives we’ve never had before,” said Elizabeth Turtle, Dragonfly principal investigator at APL. “With the capability to take images when Dragonfly is on the surface as well as while flying, DragonCam will give us both detailed views and sweeping panoramas of Titan’s landscape, as well as insight into the processes that shaped this extraordinary world. Seeing these cameras become part of the Dragonfly lander is an exciting milestone that brings us another step closer to this unprecedented exploration.”
In addition to these science cameras, Dragonfly has two navigation cameras, also built by Malin Space Science Systems, that were installed this summer.

“We are extremely pleased to have delivered the DragonCam cameras,” said Michael Ravine, DragonCam development manager and a Dragonfly co-investigator from Malin Space Science Systems. “Now to have them on the Dragonfly spacecraft, taking images, it’s so much easier to picture how they will work on Titan. These will be our eyes to see and explore this whole new world.”

Two forward-mounted cameras — a wide-angle camera (WAC) and medium-angle camera (MAC) — are designed to capture images of the terrain in front of Dragonfly. The forward WAC offers a 90-degree field of view, while the forward MAC overlaps with the WAC, capturing part of that field of view at a higher resolution. Combined, the images from these two cameras provide a stereoscopic perspective from the front of the lander. Together with two additional side-mounted WACs, the system is able to capture panoramic views of the Titan landscape.

Two downward-facing WACs provide views of the surface beneath Dragonfly, helping the mission team decide if a landing spot is safe for deploying Dragonfly’s sample-collecting tool, known as DrACO, or Drill for Acquisition of Complex Organics, and its seismometer. A high-resolution microscopic imager will aim at DrACO’s drill site to pick out the details in millimeter-sized sand grains around the sampling location.

“DragonCam will give us critical context for the samples collected by DrACO,” said Carolyn Ernst, the DragonCam instrument scientist at APL. “We’ll be collecting materials at multiple sites across Titan, and the images from the cameras will help us relate the samples to Titan’s broader landscape and piece together the story of its geology.”

Components of Dragonfly’s other instrument packages , DraGNS (Gamma-ray and Neutron Spectrometer), DraGMet (Geophysics and Meteorology), DraMS (Mass Spectrometer) and DrACO, are set for delivery, integration and testing over the next several months. Dragonfly is scheduled to launch in July 2028 and reach Titan in late 2034.

articles.title: NASA Hubble’s New View of NGC 4394 Raises the Bar
articles.dek: A brilliant galaxy with a distinct galactic bar takes center stage in this NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image.
paragraphs: A brilliant galaxy with a distinct galactic bar takes center stage in this NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image. The galaxy, called NGC 4394, is in the constellation Coma Berenices (Berenice’s Hair). At about 55 million light-years away, NGC 4394 is considered relatively nearby for a galaxy. It’s one of more than 1,000 galaxies that make up the Virgo Cluster, which is the galaxy cluster closest to us.

With its graceful spiral arms and central bar of stars, NGC 4394 closely resembles what astronomers think our home galaxy, the Milky Way, would look like if we were able to view it from a similar face-on vantage point. In a universe full of arcing spiral galaxies and nebulae organically shaped by the death and birth of stars, straight streaks of stars like NGC 4394’s galactic bar stand out. Galactic bars are extremely common; astronomers estimate 65 percent of nearby spiral galaxies have one. Hubble has imaged a wide variety of stunning barred spiral galaxies, including NGC 5728 , NGC 685 , and NGC 613 , but how do these striking features form?

Explanations for how galactic bars might form tend to center on a galaxy’s disk of stars becoming unstable. This could happen because of gravitational nudges from passing galaxies, interactions between stars, or other forces. Once the disk becomes unstable, the circular orbits of stars become elongated, leading to the barred shape seen in galaxies like NGC 4394. Observations show that galactic bars are more common among galaxies in the universe today than they were several billion years ago. Though stellar bars are in fashion today, research suggests that this is only temporary; as bars become more massive, they can themselves become unstable.

In addition to their stellar bars and spiral arms, NGC 4394 and the Milky Way galaxy share another important similarity, in that they might both contain a LINER (low-ionization nuclear emission-line region). LINER refers to an area near the center of a galaxy where its spectra feature certain ionized or neutral elements. Researchers do not yet know exactly how LINERs form, though either hungry supermassive black holes or intense star formation likely play a role.

Hubble has paid a visit to NGC 4394’s patch of sky more than once, and a previous image of NGC 4394 was released a decade ago. That image was part of an observing program (# 10515 ; PI: Peng) that focused on NGC 4394’s galactic neighbor, Messier 85 . While one of Hubble’s instruments examined Messier 85 to study its unusual collection of star clusters, another (Hubble’s Advanced Camera for Surveys ) captured a parallel area of the sky that contained NGC 4394.

Today’s image also incorporates observations from a recent program (# 18103 ; PI: Thilker) dedicated to understanding how star formation comes to an end in galaxies in dense cluster environments, and how this process differs from more isolated galaxies adrift in the field. For this observing program, researchers used Hubble’s Wide Field Camera 3 and its sensitivity to a broad wavelength range to determine the ages of individual star clusters. NGC 4394 is one of 40 galaxies they studied in this way.
Claire Andreoli NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center , Greenbelt, MD claire. andreoli@nasa. gov
Since its 1990 launch, the Hubble Space Telescope has changed our fundamental understanding of the universe.
Hubble’s most notable scientific discoveries reflect the broad range of research and the breakthroughs it has achieved.

articles.title: Prepaid electricity can make bills more predictable, but not necessarily more affordable
articles.dek: The last house I rented in Massachusetts had an oil heating tank that cost US$800 each time my roommates and I wanted to refill it.
paragraphs: The last house I rented in Massachusetts had an oil heating tank that cost US$800 each time my roommates and I wanted to refill it. If the tank ran out, there was no heat in the home, and we had to pay extra for an emergency refill and for someone to relight the pilot. A full tank of oil could last up to a month and a half – but only if we kept the heat at 55 degrees Fahrenheit (13 degrees Celsius) when we were home and cut it off when we went to work.
Where I live now, in Pennsylvania, we use natural gas and pay afterward, based on our use. It amounts to $200 to $400 monthly – and lets us keep our heat around 70 F (21 C).

Prepaying for heat in Massachusetts certainly made me more aware of how much heating a home cost, but it didn’t make energy cheaper or help me live according to modern standards. Instead, I got used to wearing my winter coat indoors. This is still a concern for many: As winter 2026 approached, some families in Maine that have oil heat had their kids sleep in snowsuits to use less fuel and keep costs down.

Most electricity companies bill for energy already used – like the natural gas company I have in Pennsylvania. But in Maryland, Baltimore Gas and Electric is proposing a prepaid electricity program , similar to my Massachusetts oil setup.

As an energy affordability researcher studying how people change their habits to use less energy when it’s expensive , the real question for me is what this type of payment system would mean for customers. Helping households manage electricity bills is different from ensuring they can afford to use enough energy at home to keep themselves safe.

BGE, which serves approximately 1. 3 million electric customers, asked Maryland Public Service Commission members to approve a prepaid program for customers in July 2026. The company says this would help people keep a better handle on their energy spending .

Rather than getting a monthly bill, customers who opted into the plan would make an initial $40 payment toward future electricity use . They could then monitor their power usage and get alerts when balances run low.

The utility’s vice president of regulatory policy and strategy, John Frain, told the Maryland Public Service Commission that prepaid customers wouldn’t have to pay security deposits to open new accounts and wouldn’t have to worry about late payment or reconnection fees if service were disconnected because they weren’t able to pay their bills.

For customers with unpaid balances of up to $1,000, the company would have 25% of each prepayment applied to previous debts and 75% go toward future electricity costs. The company expects to save a yet-undetermined amount of money on collection efforts.
Consumer advocates warn that prepaid billing could cause problems for customers while making life easier for the utility company.
For instance, people on fixed incomes, such as Social Security, could experience increased mental stress because of frequent fears their electricity might be cut off .

They also might make significant changes in their lifestyles: A 2014 study in New Zealand found customers who prepaid for their electricity rationed their own power by, for instance, turning on an electric water heater only every third day and taking cold showers on other days.

Because Maryland prepaid customers would pay the same electricity rates as everyone else, any bill savings would likely come from living without many of the basic services electricity brings to modern life .

The company’s response to this concern is that while customers whose balance gets to zero will be disconnected – as soon as the next day – they’ll have an easier time getting reconnected . Once people add $15 to their account, power can be restored in less than 30 minutes .

But even short disconnections can cause big problems. For people dependent on electric-powered medical devices, such as breathing equipment or home dialysis machines , getting disconnected can injure or kill them. Without the power to charge a phone or power a Wi-Fi router, some people may have trouble getting alerts about their balance or making payments to turn their electricity back on.

Under traditional billing, Maryland law gives customers protections against rapid disconnections. When people are late paying their bills, utilities have to notify them of the overdue balance and give them at least 14 days to pay before cutting off power – a period during which they can still use electricity.
This delay gives people a chance to make payment arrangements and seek financial assistance , such as from the state’s Office of Home Energy Programs .
Applying to that office allows customers to request an additional 55-day reprieve from disconnection , which can help families stay connected during extreme weather events.
In August 2019, BGE conducted a trial run of the prepaid system with 527 customers.

An independent analysis found that power disconnections were often shorter – five hours on average – for prepaid customers than for customers who were billed later for the power they used, whose power was off for an average of 9. 4 days. But 10% of prepaid customers had their power cut off at some point during the test period, compared with just 1% of those in the traditional billing program.

The trial run generated some positive outcomes for customers: 61% of the participants said they had better control over their energy bills by being able to decide when and how much to prepay, and 34% said the program’s feature of progressively paying off overdue bills helped them.
However, 41% of participants left before the program formally ended in November 2020. Among those who left , one-third didn’t like making frequent payments, and 23% felt their energy cost more.
BGE told Maryland officials that the prepaid program is “ not intended as a cost-savings program for customers .”
The company says its prepay program offers customers online tools to monitor their energy use and the option to make payments when it’s financially convenient.

articles.title: California raised minimum wages for fast-food workers – here’s how it played out 2 years later
articles.dek: Even before the 2026 midterm elections delivered a clear message about cost-of-living concerns, many states had been raising their minimum wage on their own as one way to…
paragraphs: Even before the 2026 midterm elections delivered a clear message about cost-of-living concerns, many states had been raising their minimum wage on their own as one way to increase workers’ purchasing power. And some have taken a more targeted approach, setting wage floors for specific industries.
As the example of California shows, however, these initiatives can produce mixed results.

In April 2024, California began requiring fast-food chains with at least 60 locations nationwide to pay a minimum wage of US$20 an hour, $4 above the statewide minimum at the time. The governor’s office estimated that more than 500,000 workers would be covered by this mandate.

As a researcher of health and labor markets , I joined with economists David Neumark , Gary Wagner and Vitor Melo to run a study measuring the impact on California’s fast-food industry – specifically, whether restaurants employed fewer workers because of the ensuing higher labor costs.
We found that the answer depends on which establishments you look at.

For the state as a whole, the law didn’t affect employment in any statistically detectable way, we concluded. But smaller chains did take a hit, with employment falling by roughly 20%, while the number of locations dropped by about 10%. New openings fell by 17%-20%, and closures rose by 9%-21%.
This employment decline comes almost entirely from fast-food chains ceasing to operate in California, rather than from staffing cuts at the locations that remain.

The impact of minimum wage hikes holds importance far beyond the fast-food sector. Their proponents point to the fact that the federal minimum wage of $7. 25 an hour has stayed unchanged since 2009 and argue that states and municipalities need to take action on their own.

Los Angeles is phasing in a $30 wage for hotel and airport workers, while California’s healthcare workers just received another scheduled increase . Vermont lawmakers have proposed a $20 fast-food wage of their own.
In addition, a total of 16 states will raise their minimum wages across the board on Jan. 1, 2027.
The question of whether and how minimum wages affect employment still provokes a vigorous debate among economists.

In California’s case, some researchers have found that lifting the minimum wage caused small declines in employment compared with other states; others contend that the effect on jobs is essentially zero.
More broadly, some researchers have found that minimum wage hikes cost jobs. But the time horizon matters, and effects tend to get larger in the long run .

Our study didn’t try to settle that disagreement. Instead, we wanted to find out how employers did adjust, and whether large and small chains responded differently. What happens when higher minimum wages raise one sector’s costs and prices while its closest substitutes – such as sit-down restaurants – keep paying the lower statewide minimum wage?

We relied on a database that recorded every business location in the country by name, along with the number of employed workers, each year. That let us directly identify the chains that were subject to California’s law, count each chains’ national footprint to apply the 60-location rule, and track outcomes from 2019 through 2025: total employment, employment at locations that stayed open, the number of locations, and openings and closures.

We also compared California with other states and separately compared each chain’s California restaurants with the same chain’s restaurants elsewhere. Finally, we divided the covered chains into two groups: The 20 largest, which account for about 60% of covered jobs, and the 261 smaller ones.

For the state as a whole, we found that employment at covered restaurants was basically unchanged, and employment at restaurants that stayed open didn’t change. Among the 20 largest chains, there was no detectable effect at all for any of the measures we tracked over this period.
But the smaller chains tell a different story, recording substantial declines in employment, locations and openings, while closures rose.

How to reconcile the flat statewide numbers with the sharp effects on smaller chains? The largest chains employ most of the workers affected by the new minimum wage rule, so the statewide total is dominated by them. And the reduced entry and higher exit among smaller chains may have eased competitive pressure on the largest ones.

A final point: The biggest chains tend to be the most automated, relying more on equipment such as self-serve kiosks that can reduce the number of workers needed. That may help explain the muted employment response among these larger businesses.

First, we caution that the absence of a clear short-run effect on total employment doesn’t prove that the policy won’t cause bigger job losses over time as companies adapt to the new law. We also can’t answer what happened to the workers at the most affected restaurants or what happened to prices at those establishments, although other research suggests they rose by 3% to 4%.

That said, the law was implemented barely 2½ years ago, and some of the larger effects that economists might expect – such as the closure of labor-intensive restaurants or fewer openings – are already apparent among smaller chains.

Second, it’s important to remember that California’s fast-food minimum wage applies only to chains with 60 or more locations. So the smaller chains in that range likely lack the scale, automation and pricing power of the national brands and are most sensitive to the new wage floor. Indeed, the law appears to have shifted California’s fast-food market toward its largest chains, a pattern that other researchers documented in a similar study that looked at Germany’s national minimum wage.

For the cities and states now weighing wage floors of their own, the California evidence isn’t a slam dunk either way. It shows that the costs, broadly speaking, fall first on the smaller chains covered by the law – but whether it meaningfully impacts the largest chains is unclear.
